narrative:
The 2025 St. Louis Cardinals opened the season with the push-and-pull rhythm that would define their entire year. On Opening Day, Ryan Fernandez was torched for a devastating triple that plated multiple runs, only for Nolan Arenado to answer with a clutch single that kept the Cardinals competitive. That seesaw pattern — a gut punch followed by a defiant response — became the team's signature in April, with Willson Contreras and Pedro Pagés delivering timely extra-base hits while the bullpen, led by a shaky Ryan Helsley, gave too many leads back. The month ended with Arenado's solo shot saving a critical late-inning situation, but the Cardinals were already treading water.

May and early June brought little relief on the pitching side, as Steven Matz and Andre Pallante continued to struggle in high-leverage moments, surrendering triples and home runs at the worst possible times. Yet amid the turbulence, a surprising hero emerged: backup catcher Iván Herrera. His two massive home runs in June — a two-run shot on June 5th worth over 0.60 WPA and a three-run blast on June 9th worth 0.667, the most impactful positive play of the entire season — briefly ignited hope that the Cardinals might claw back into relevance. Arenado, ever the steadying presence, reached double digits in home runs during this stretch, and the offense showed flashes of the firepower that could have made this team dangerous.

The summer months told a grimmer story. A Kyle Leahy grand slam surrender in mid-June and a catastrophic Phil Maton blow in July — a three-run homer by Sean Murphy that flipped a game entirely — epitomized a bullpen that could not hold leads. Jordan Walker and Brendan Donovan provided genuine offensive bright spots in August, with Walker's line-drive single and Donovan's 25th double carrying real weight in wins. But for every rally, a JoJo Romero meltdown or a Riley O'Brien double-up erased the progress. The Cardinals were a team spinning its wheels, talented enough to compete on individual nights but too inconsistent across the rotation and relief corps to string together the winning streaks a playoff push demands.

September confirmed what the standings had been whispering all summer. A backbreaking double play by Brendan Donovan on September 20th killed a late rally, and Riley O'Brien's continued struggles in relief kept the losses piling up. Even Donovan's 31st double in the final week felt more like a footnote than a comeback catalyst. The Cardinals finished 78-84, outscored by 65 runs on the season, victims of a league-average offense that could never compensate for a pitching staff that ranked among the worst in the National League. With a 4.29 ERA and an OPS of just .693, St. Louis was simply not built to win in 2025, and the absence of playoff baseball at Busch Stadium reflected a roster in need of significant retooling heading into the offseason.

chapters.title: Opening Skirmishes
chapters.description: The Cardinals trade blows with opponents in a volatile April, with Arenado and Contreras keeping the team afloat despite early pitching concerns.

chapters.title: Herrera's Spark
chapters.description: Iván Herrera emerges as an unlikely hero with back-to-back massive home runs, giving the Cardinals their brightest offensive moments of the season.

chapters.title: Summer Erosion
chapters.description: A brutal mid-summer stretch sees the bullpen implode repeatedly, with grand slams and late-inning meltdowns extinguishing any playoff hopes.

chapters.title: Too Little, Too Late
chapters.description: Walker and Donovan deliver clutch hits in August but cannot overcome a roster-wide lack of consistency as the Cardinals slide toward a losing record.

chapters.title: A Season Fades Away
chapters.description: September brings double plays, blown leads, and late doubles that amount to moral victories as St. Louis finishes six games under .500 and well outside the playoff picture.
